smt-2023-power-1-01.title: Circle best responses
smt-2023-power-1-01.body:
Player 1's best response to $X$ is $A$ ($10>7$); to $Y$ it is $B$ ($-2>-5$). Player 2's best response to $A$ is $X$ ($7>1$); to $B$ it is $Y$ ($-3>-8$).

A profile is a mutual best response when both coordinates are best responses to each other: $(A,X)$ and $(B,Y)$.

**Answer: $(A,X)$ and $(B,Y)$**

smt-2023-power-1-02.title: Circle best responses
smt-2023-power-1-02.body:
Player 1 (maximize over the rows within each column): column $X$ has payoffs $5,5,3$, so best responses are $A$ and $B$; column $Y$ has $1,0,1$: $A$ and $C$; column $Z$ has $7,7,5$: $A$ and $B$.

Player 2 (maximize over columns within each row): row $A$ has $-3,0,-1$: $Y$; row $B$ has $1,0,1$: $X$ and $Z$; row $C$ has $10,-1,7$: $X$.

Cells where both players' payoffs are best responses: $(B,X)$, $(A,Y)$, $(B,Z)$.

**Answer: $(B,X)$, $(A,Y)$, $(B,Z)$**

smt-2023-power-1-03.title: Unpack both definitions
smt-2023-power-1-03.body:
Fix a profile $(a_1,a_2)$.

Player 1 has no profitable deviation iff $u_1(a_1,a_2)\ge u_1(a_1',a_2)$ for every row $a_1'$, i.e. iff $u_1(a_1,a_2)$ is a maximum of its column, i.e. iff Player 1's payoff in this cell is circled.

Similarly Player 2 has no profitable deviation iff $u_2(a_1,a_2)\ge u_2(a_1,a_2')$ for every column $a_2'$, iff Player 2's payoff in this cell is circled.

So $(a_1,a_2)$ is a Nash equilibrium iff neither player has a profitable deviation iff both payoffs in its cell are circled. Hence the doubly circled cells are exactly the pure Nash equilibria. $\blacksquare$

smt-2023-power-1-04.title: Describe the tree
smt-2023-power-1-04.body:
- **Root:** a node labelled $1$ with two edges $A$ and $B$.
- **After $A$:** a node labelled $2$ with three edges $R,P,S$ (player two's throw). Below each of these, a node labelled $3$ with three edges $R,P,S$ (player three's throw, made after seeing player two's).
- **After $B$:** a node labelled $3$ with three edges $R,P,S$. Below each, a node labelled $2$ with three edges $R,P,S$.
- That gives $9$ terminal nodes under $A$ and $9$ under $B$, $18$ in all. Payoffs are listed in the order (player one, player two, player three): if the two throws are equal, $(1,0,0)$; if player two's throw beats player three's (rock beats scissors, scissors beats paper, paper beats rock), $(0,1,-1)$; if player three's throw beats player two's, $(0,-1,1)$.

For example, the path $A,R,S$ (player two throws rock, player three throws scissors) ends at $(0,1,-1)$, and the path $B,P,P$ ends at $(1,0,0)$.

smt-2023-power-1-05a.title: Multiply the number of options at each of Player 1's nodes
smt-2023-power-1-05a.body:
Player 1 moves at six nodes, with action sets $\{A,B,C\}$, $\{D\}$, $\{E,F,G\}$, $\{H\}$, $\{I,J\}$ and $\{K,L\}$, i.e. $3,1,3,1,2,2$ options. A strategy picks one at every node, so there are $3\cdot1\cdot3\cdot1\cdot2\cdot2=36$ strategies.

**Answer: 36**

smt-2023-power-1-05b.title: Multiply the number of options at each of Player 2's nodes
smt-2023-power-1-05b.body:
Player 2 moves at four nodes: the root $\{a,b\}$, the node after $E$ with $\{g,h\}$, the node after $C$ with $\{c,d,e\}$, and the node after $D$ with $\{f\}$. That gives $2\cdot2\cdot3\cdot1=12$ strategies.

**Answer: 12**

smt-2023-power-1-06.title: Best responses
smt-2023-power-1-06.body:
Firm two's strategies are Fight and Share; firm one's are Enter and Don't. Payoffs: (Enter, Fight): $(-1,-1)$; (Enter, Share): $(2,2)$; (Don't, Fight) and (Don't, Share): $(0,5)$ (firm two's choice is never made).

Best responses: Firm one's best response to Fight is Don't ($0>-1$); to Share it is Enter ($2>0$). Firm two's best response to Enter is Share ($2>-1$); to Don't both Fight and Share give $5$, so both are best responses.

Mutual best responses: (Enter, Share), and (Don't, Fight). (Don't, Share) is not an equilibrium since firm one would then Enter.

**Answer: (Enter, Share) and (Don't, Fight)**

smt-2023-power-1-07.title: Backward induction
smt-2023-power-1-07.body:
The subgame starting after Enter is a one-player decision for firm two: Share gives $2$, Fight gives $-1$, so firm two must play Share there. Knowing this, firm one compares Enter ($2$) with Don't ($0$) and plays Enter. The only SPE is (Enter, Share). (The Nash equilibrium (Don't, Fight) is not subgame perfect: Fight is a non-credible threat.)

**Answer: (Enter, Share)**

smt-2023-power-1-08.title: The game is its own subgame
smt-2023-power-1-08.body: The subgame starting at the root node is the entire game. By the definition of an SPE, the strategies restricted to every subgame, in particular this one, form a Nash equilibrium. Hence an SPE is a Nash equilibrium of the whole game. $\blacksquare$

smt-2023-power-1-09.title: Backward induction
smt-2023-power-1-09.body:
In the subgame after $A$, Player 2 compares $0$ ($a$) and $15$ ($b$): plays $b$. After $B$: $16$ ($e$) vs $20$ ($f$): plays $f$. After $C$: $3$ ($h$) vs $3$ ($i$): indifferent, so either is a Nash equilibrium of that subgame.

Player 1 anticipates this and compares: $A\to5$, $B\to16$, $C\to1$ (if $h$) or $7$ (if $i$). In both cases $B$ is best.

So there are two SPE: $(B,(b,f,h))$ and $(B,(b,f,i))$, both with outcome $B,f$ and payoffs $(16,20)$.

**Answer: $(B,(b,f,h))$ and $(B,(b,f,i))$**

smt-2023-power-1-10.title: Induction on the length of the longest path
smt-2023-power-1-10.body:
**Yes.** We prove by induction on $n$, the number of moves in the longest path of the tree, that every such game has an SPE.

*Base case $n=1$.* Only one decision node (the root) with terminal children: the player who moves picks an action with the largest payoff for themselves. This is a Nash equilibrium of the game, and the only subgame is the game itself, so it is an SPE.

*Inductive step.* Suppose every game whose longest path has at most $n$ moves has an SPE, and take a game $G$ whose longest path has $n+1$ moves. Call a decision node *last* if all its children are terminal. The subgame at a last node is a one-move game: the mover picks an action with the largest payoff for themselves (ties broken arbitrarily). Fix such a choice $\sigma_\ell$ at every last node $\ell$, and let $G'$ be the game obtained by replacing each last node $\ell$ by a terminal node with the payoffs of the chosen action. The longest path of $G'$ has at most $n$ moves, so $G'$ has an SPE $\sigma'$. Let $\sigma$ be $\sigma'$ together with the choices $\sigma_\ell$.

We claim $\sigma$ is an SPE of $G$. At a last node this is true by construction. Let $d$ be any other decision node and suppose a player $i$ deviates in the subgame $G_d$ to a strategy $\tau$. Modify $\tau$ at the last nodes where $i$ moves, replacing it with $\sigma_\ell$; this does not decrease $i$'s payoff, because $\sigma_\ell$ is a best action for the mover at $\ell$ given what follows. The modified deviation is a deviation in the subgame $G'_d$ of $G'$ (with last nodes replaced by their payoffs), where $\sigma'$ is a Nash equilibrium, so it is not profitable. Hence the original deviation was not profitable either, and $\sigma$ is a Nash equilibrium of every subgame of $G$. $\blacksquare$

smt-2023-power-1-11.title: A counterexample
smt-2023-power-1-11.body: **No.** Consider a game in which Player 1 has two actions, $X$ and $Y$, each ending the game with the same payoff, say $1$. The only subgame is the whole game, and each of "play $X$" and "play $Y$" is a Nash equilibrium of it (no deviation changes the payoff). So both are SPE, and they induce different outcomes ($X$ versus $Y$). $\blacksquare$

smt-2023-power-1-12.title: Use the magic square
smt-2023-power-1-12.body:
Label the nine squares with the numbers of the magic square
$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|}\hline 2&7&6\\\hline 9&5&1\\\hline 4&3&8\\\hline\end{array}$$
This is a bijection between squares and the numbers $1,\dots,9$. Every row, column and long diagonal of the grid sums to $15$, so each of the $8$ winning lines is a triple of distinct numbers with sum $15$.

Conversely, the triples of distinct numbers from $\{1,\dots,9\}$ with sum $15$ are exactly $\{1,5,9\},\{1,6,8\},\{2,4,9\},\{2,5,8\},\{2,6,7\},\{3,4,8\},\{3,5,7\},\{4,5,6\}$. These are the $8$ lines of the grid: rows $\{2,7,6\},\{9,5,1\},\{4,3,8\}$, columns $\{2,9,4\},\{7,5,3\},\{6,1,8\}$, diagonals $\{2,5,8\},\{6,5,4\}$.

So under the bijection square $\leftrightarrow$ number, a set of squares contains a winning line iff the corresponding set of numbers contains a triple with sum $15$. The two games have the same turn order, the same winning conditions and the same tie condition, and the correspondence maps every position (set of chosen squares for each player) to the corresponding position and each legal move to the corresponding legal move. So it maps strategies to strategies bijectively (a strategy is a choice of move at every position of a player) and preserves the payoffs (win, tie, lose). Hence the games are equivalent. $\blacksquare$

smt-2023-power-1-13.title: Invert the bijections
smt-2023-power-1-13.body:
($\Rightarrow$) Suppose the normal form game is equivalent to the extensive form game via bijections $h_i:A_i\to S_i$ with $u(a_1,\dots,a_n)=u'(h_1(a_1),\dots,h_n(a_n))$. Bijections have inverses, so define $g_i=h_i^{-1}:S_i\to A_i$, which is a bijection. For any strategy profile $(s_1,\dots,s_n)$, put $a_i=g_i(s_i)$, so $h_i(a_i)=s_i$; then $u'(s_1,\dots,s_n)=u'(h_1(a_1),\dots,h_n(a_n))=u(a_1,\dots,a_n)=u(g_1(s_1),\dots,g_n(s_n))$. That is exactly the definition of the extensive form game being equivalent to the normal form game.

($\Leftarrow$) The same argument with the roles reversed: given bijections $g_i$ satisfying the second condition, $h_i=g_i^{-1}$ satisfy the first. $\blacksquare$

smt-2023-power-1-14.title: Define the normal form from strategies
smt-2023-power-1-14.body: **Yes.** Given a two-player extensive form game with strategy spaces $S_1,S_2$ and payoffs $u_i(s_1,s_2)$ (the payoff at the terminal node reached when both players follow their strategies), define the normal form game with action sets $A_1=S_1$, $A_2=S_2$ and payoffs $u_i'(a_1,a_2)=u_i(a_1,a_2)$. Take $g_i$ to be the identity map $S_i\to A_i$ (a bijection). Then $u(s_1,s_2)=u'(g_1(s_1),g_2(s_2))$ for all strategy profiles, so the two games are equivalent. $\blacksquare$

smt-2023-power-1-15.title: Compare pure Nash equilibria
smt-2023-power-1-15.body:
**No.** Consider the *matching parity game*: each player chooses $1$ or $2$. If the numbers have the same parity, Player 1 gets $1$ and Player 2 gets $0$; otherwise Player 2 gets $1$ and Player 1 gets $0$.

This game has no pure Nash equilibrium: in a profile with equal parity Player 2 can deviate and get $1$ instead of $0$; in a profile with different parity Player 1 can deviate and get $1$ instead of $0$.

Suppose it were equivalent to some finite extensive form game. By Problem 1.10 (backward induction) the extensive game has a Subgame Perfect Nash Equilibrium, which by Problem 1.8 is a Nash equilibrium, in pure strategies. An equivalence is a payoff-preserving bijection of the strategy spaces, so it carries Nash equilibria to Nash equilibria. Then the matching parity game would have a pure Nash equilibrium, a contradiction. $\blacksquare$

(Alternatively, by counting: if one player moves second after seeing a move with $2$ options, their strategy space has $4$ elements, but the normal form has only $2$ actions per player.)

smt-2023-power-2-01.title: Circle best responses
smt-2023-power-2-01.body:
By Problem 1.3 every pure Nash equilibrium is a cell where both payoffs are circled. In the matrix
$$\begin{array}{c|ccc} & R & P & S\\ \hline R & (0,0) & (-1,1) & (1,-1)\\ P & (1,-1) & (0,0) & (-1,1)\\ S & (-1,1) & (1,-1) & (0,0)\end{array}$$
Player 1's best responses are: $P$ against $R$, $S$ against $P$, $R$ against $S$; Player 2's best responses are the move that beats Player 1's. No cell has both circled, since a best response to $R$ is $P$ (not $R$), etc.

Directly: in any profile, either it is a draw (then either player can switch to the move beating the other's and win) or someone loses (the loser can switch to a move that beats the winner's move). So every profile has a profitable deviation. $\blacksquare$

smt-2023-power-2-02.title: Compute the expected payoff
smt-2023-power-2-02.body:
Against the uniform mixed strategy of player one, any pure move of player two wins with probability $\frac13$, draws with probability $\frac13$ and loses with probability $\frac13$, so its expected payoff is $\frac13\cdot1+\frac13\cdot0+\frac13\cdot(-1)=0$.

If player two plays rock, paper, scissors with probabilities $r,p,1-r-p$, the expected payoff is $r\cdot0+p\cdot0+(1-r-p)\cdot0=0$, independent of $r,p$. So no strategy gives player two more than $0$, which is what the uniform strategy gives. $\blacksquare$

smt-2023-power-2-03.title: Evaluate the double sum
smt-2023-power-2-03.body: $U_1(\delta_a,\delta_b)=\sum_{x\in A_1}\sum_{y\in A_2}\delta_a(x)\delta_b(y)u_1(x,y)$. Since $\delta_a(x)=0$ for $x\ne a$ and $\delta_b(y)=0$ for $y\neq b$, only the term $x=a$, $y=b$ survives, and it equals $1\cdot1\cdot u_1(a,b)$. The argument for $U_2$ is identical. $\blacksquare$

smt-2023-power-2-04.title: Weighted average argument
smt-2023-power-2-04.body:
Let $m=U_1(p_1,p_{-1})$. Since $p_1$ is a best response, no deviation to a point mass can do better: $U_1(\delta_x,p_{-1})\le m$ for every $x\in A_1$.

But $m=\sum_x p_1(x)U_1(\delta_x,p_{-1})$ with weights $p_1(x)\ge0$ summing to $1$. If some $x$ with $p_1(x)>0$ had $U_1(\delta_x,p_{-1})<m$, then, as all other terms are at most $m$, the weighted average would be strictly less than $m$, a contradiction. So $U_1(\delta_x,p_{-1})=m$ whenever $p_1(x)>0$; in particular for $x=a$ and $x=b$. $\blacksquare$

smt-2023-power-2-05.title: Indifference conditions
smt-2023-power-2-05.body:
In a mixed equilibrium where both players mix, each is indifferent between their two actions (Problem 2.4).

Player 1 indifferent between $A$ and $B$: $10p_2(X)+4p_2(Y)=2p_2(X)+5p_2(Y)$. With $p_2(Y)=1-p_2(X)$: $4+6p_2(X)=5-3p_2(X)$, so $p_2(X)=\frac19$.

Player 2 indifferent between $X$ and $Y$: $8p_1(A)+3p_1(B)=p_1(A)+7p_1(B)$. With $p_1(B)=1-p_1(A)$: $3+5p_1(A)=7-6p_1(A)$, so $p_1(A)=\frac4{11}$.

Equilibrium: $p_1=\left(\frac4{11},\frac7{11}\right)$ on $(A,B)$ and $p_2=\left(\frac19,\frac89\right)$ on $(X,Y)$. (The game also has two pure equilibria, $(A,X)$ and $(B,Y)$, which are mixed equilibria in point masses; the one above is the equilibrium where both players mix.)

**Answer: $p_1=(\frac4{11},\frac7{11})$, $p_2=(\frac19,\frac89)$**

smt-2023-power-2-06.title: All three actions indifferent
smt-2023-power-2-06.body:
Look for an equilibrium in which every action is used. By Problem 2.4 each player is indifferent among all three of their actions.

Player 1: $2q_X-q_Y+7q_Z=q_X+0q_Y+7q_Z=3q_X+q_Y+5q_Z$, where $q=p_2$. The first equality gives $q_X=q_Y$; the second then gives $q_Z=\frac32q_X$. With $q_X+q_Y+q_Z=1$: $q=\left(\frac27,\frac27,\frac37\right)$. Each action then yields $\frac{23}7$.

Player 2: $-3p_A-p_B+10p_C=0p_A+5p_B+4p_C=-p_A+p_B+7p_C$, where $p=p_1$. Solving gives $p=\left(\frac25,\frac15,\frac25\right)$; each action yields $\frac{13}5$.

Since all supports are full and both players are indifferent, neither can improve: this is a mixed strategy Nash equilibrium. (This game has other equilibria too, e.g. the pure profile $(C,X)$; the official answer is the fully mixed one above.)

**Answer: $p_1=(\frac25,\frac15,\frac25)$, $p_2=(\frac27,\frac27,\frac37)$**

smt-2023-power-2-07.title: Renormalize
smt-2023-power-2-07.body:
Let $t=p_i(a_i)>0$. We cannot have $t=1$, since then $p_i=\delta_{a_i}$ and $U_i(p_i,\cdot)>U_i(\delta_{a_i},\cdot)$ would be absurd. Define $p_i'(x)=\frac{p_i(x)}{1-t}$ for $x\ne a_i$ and $p_i'(a_i)=0$. This is a probability distribution, and $p_i=t\,\delta_{a_i}+(1-t)\,p_i'$.

Fix any $p_{-i}$ for which $U_i(p_i,p_{-i})>U_i(\delta_{a_i},p_{-i})$. By linearity of $U_i$ in the player's own strategy,
$$U_i(p_i,p_{-i})=t\,U_i(\delta_{a_i},p_{-i})+(1-t)\,U_i(p_i',p_{-i}).$$
The inequality becomes $(1-t)U_i(p_i',p_{-i})>(1-t)U_i(\delta_{a_i},p_{-i})$, i.e. $U_i(p_i',p_{-i})>U_i(\delta_{a_i},p_{-i})$. So $p_i'$, which never plays $a_i$, does strictly better than $a_i$ against every such $p_{-i}$ (and it is the same $p_i'$ whenever the original $p_i$ was). $\blacksquare$

smt-2023-power-2-08.title: Both directions
smt-2023-power-2-08.body:
($\Rightarrow$) Let $a_i$ be dominated, and let $q_i$ be any mixed strategy with $q_i(a_i)=c>0$ and $p_{-i}$ any opponent strategy. Choose $p_i$ with $U_i(p_i,p_{-i})>U_i(\delta_{a_i},p_{-i})$. Let $q_i'=q_i-c\,\delta_{a_i}+c\,p_i$, which is a probability distribution (the weight $c$ on $a_i$ is moved to $p_i$). By linearity, $U_i(q_i',p_{-i})-U_i(q_i,p_{-i})=c\left(U_i(p_i,p_{-i})-U_i(\delta_{a_i},p_{-i})\right)>0$. So $q_i$ is not a best response to $p_{-i}$. Hence $a_i$ is never played with positive probability in a best response.

($\Leftarrow$) Suppose $a_i$ is not dominated. Then there is an opponent strategy $p_{-i}$ for which no $p_i$ satisfies $U_i(p_i,p_{-i})>U_i(\delta_{a_i},p_{-i})$, i.e. $U_i(\delta_{a_i},p_{-i})\ge U_i(p_i,p_{-i})$ for all $p_i$. So $\delta_{a_i}$, which plays $a_i$ with probability $1$, is a best response to $p_{-i}$. Thus $a_i$ is played with positive probability in some best response. By contraposition, if $a_i$ is never in any best response, it is dominated. $\blacksquare$

smt-2023-power-2-09.title: One parameter each
smt-2023-power-2-09.body: A mixed strategy of player one is determined by $q_1=p_1(a_1)\in[0,1]$, and $p_1(a_2)=1-q_1$; conversely every $q_1\in[0,1]$ gives a valid distribution. So player one's mixed strategies correspond bijectively to the closed interval $[0,1]$. Likewise for player two with $q_2$. $\blacksquare$

smt-2023-power-2-11.title: Explicit epsilon-delta
smt-2023-power-2-11.body:
Let $M=|v_{11}|+|v_{12}|+|v_{21}|+|v_{22}|$ and write $V=\sum w_{jk}(q_1,q_2)v_{jk}$ with the four weights $w_{11}=q_1q_2$, $w_{12}=q_1(1-q_2)$, $w_{21}=(1-q_1)q_2$, $w_{22}=(1-q_1)(1-q_2)$. Each weight is a product $s\cdot t$ with $s\in\{q_1,1-q_1\}$ and $t\in\{q_2,1-q_2\}$, both in $[0,1]$. For another point $(q_1',q_2')$, with corresponding $s',t'$, we have $|st-s't'|\le|s-s'|\,t+s'\,|t-t'|\le|q_1-q_1'|+|q_2-q_2'|$.

Fix $\epsilon>0$ and $\delta=\frac{\epsilon}{2M+1}$. If the distance between $(q_1',q_2')$ and $(q_1,q_2)$ is less than $\delta$, then $|q_1-q_1'|<\delta$ and $|q_2-q_2'|<\delta$, so
$$|V(q_1',q_2')-V(q_1,q_2)|\le\sum|w_{jk}-w_{jk}'||v_{jk}|\le 2\delta M<\epsilon.$$ $\blacksquare$

smt-2023-power-2-12.title: Linearity in each variable
smt-2023-power-2-12.body:
Fix $q_2$. Expanding, $V(q_1,q_2)=q_1\,\alpha(q_2)+\beta(q_2)$ with $\alpha(q_2)=q_2v_{11}+(1-q_2)v_{12}-q_2v_{21}-(1-q_2)v_{22}$ and $\beta(q_2)=q_2v_{21}+(1-q_2)v_{22}$, constants with respect to $q_1$. Then $f(q_1)=\alpha q_1+\beta$ satisfies
$$f(tq_1+(1-t)q_1')=\alpha(tq_1+(1-t)q_1')+\beta=t(\alpha q_1+\beta)+(1-t)(\alpha q_1'+\beta)=tf(q_1)+(1-t)f(q_1'),$$
so the convexity inequality holds with equality: $V$ is convex in $q_1$.

Similarly, fixing $q_1$, $V=q_2\,\gamma(q_1)+\eta(q_1)$ is affine in $q_2$, so $-V$ is convex in $q_2$, i.e. $V$ is concave in $q_2$. $\blacksquare$

smt-2023-power-2-13.title: Apply the facts
smt-2023-power-2-13.body:
By Problems 2.9, 2.11 and 2.12, $V$ is a continuous function on $[0,1]\times[0,1]$ that is convex in $q_1$ and concave in $q_2$. So the Min-Max Theorem gives $v:=\max_{q_1}\min_{q_2}V=\min_{q_2}\max_{q_1}V$.

By Fact 1 there is $q_1^*$ attaining the maximum in $\max_{q_1}\min_{q_2}V$ (so $\min_{q_2}V(q_1^*,q_2)=v$) and $q_2^*$ attaining the minimum in $\min_{q_2}\max_{q_1}V$ (so $\max_{q_1}V(q_1,q_2^*)=v$). Then
$$v=\min_{q_2}V(q_1^*,q_2)\le V(q_1^*,q_2^*)\le\max_{q_1}V(q_1,q_2^*)=v,$$
so $V(q_1^*,q_2^*)=v$, as required. $\blacksquare$

smt-2023-power-2-14.title: Check both players
smt-2023-power-2-14.body:
Let $v$ denote the common value, so $q_1^*$ is a maximizer of $q_1\mapsto\min_{q_2}V(q_1,q_2)$ and $q_2^*$ a minimizer of $q_2\mapsto\max_{q_1}V(q_1,q_2)$ (this is how they were chosen), with $V(q_1^*,q_2^*)=v$.

*Player one:* for every $q_1$, $V(q_1,q_2^*)\le\max_{q_1'}V(q_1',q_2^*)=v=V(q_1^*,q_2^*)$. So player one cannot gain by deviating from $q_1^*$.

*Player two:* her payoff is $-V$, so a deviation to $q_2$ is profitable iff $V(q_1^*,q_2)<V(q_1^*,q_2^*)$. But $V(q_1^*,q_2)\ge\min_{q_2'}V(q_1^*,q_2')=v=V(q_1^*,q_2^*)$. So no profitable deviation exists.

Hence $(q_1^*,q_2^*)$ is a Nash equilibrium. $\blacksquare$

smt-2023-power-3-01.title: Write the cases
smt-2023-power-3-01.body:
$$u_i(b_1,\dots,b_n)=\begin{cases}v_i-\max_{j\ne i}b_j & \text{if } b_i>b_j\text{ for all }j\ne i\ (\text{agent } i \text{ has the highest bid}),\\ 0&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}$$
(The price the winner pays is the second highest bid, which is the highest of the other agents' bids.)

smt-2023-power-3-02.title: Deviate to bidding their value
smt-2023-power-3-02.body: Agent $i$'s utility is $v_i-p<0$. The highest bid among the others is $p>v_i$. If agent $i$ instead bids $b_i'=v_i<p$, they lose the auction, and their utility becomes $0>v_i-p$. So this is a profitable deviation. $\blacksquare$

smt-2023-power-3-03.title: Consider every deviation
smt-2023-power-3-03.body: Currently the utility is $v_i-p\ge0$, where $p$ is the highest bid among the others. Any deviation (the others' bids stay fixed) either (a) loses, giving utility $0\le v_i-p$, or (b) still wins, in which case the price is still the highest other bid $p$ (it does not depend on $i$'s own bid), giving utility $v_i-p$ again. In neither case is the utility strictly higher, so agent $i$ has no profitable deviation. $\blacksquare$

smt-2023-power-3-04.title: Truthful bidding
smt-2023-power-3-04.body:
Let every agent bid their value: $b_i=v_i$. The agent $w$ with the largest value wins and pays the second largest value, which is less than $v_w$ (values are distinct).

*The winner* has payoff $v_w-p\ge0$ with $p\le v_w$, so by Problem 3.3 has no profitable deviation.

*A loser $i$* has utility $0$. To win, they would have to bid more than the highest other bid, which is at least $v_w>v_i$, and then they would pay at least $v_w>v_i$, for a negative utility. So no deviation is profitable.

Hence bidding one's value is a Nash equilibrium. $\blacksquare$

smt-2023-power-3-06.title: Shade the bid
smt-2023-power-3-06.body: Agent $i$ bids $v_i$ and wins, with utility $v_i-v_i=0$. Let $b'<v_i$ be the highest other bid (it is strictly lower since bids are separated). If agent $i$ bids $\frac{v_i+b'}{2}\in(b',v_i)$, they still win, now paying $\frac{v_i+b'}2<v_i$, for utility $\frac{v_i-b'}2>0$. This is a profitable deviation. $\blacksquare$

smt-2023-power-3-07.title: Maximize a quadratic
smt-2023-power-3-07.body:
$u_1(q_1,q_2^*)=\left(22-2(q_1+q_2^*)\right)q_1-6q_1=q_1(16-2q_1-2q_2^*)=-2q_1\left(q_1-(8-q_2^*)\right)$. This quadratic is maximized at the midpoint of its roots $0$ and $8-q_2^*$: $q_1=4-\frac{q_2^*}2$ (if this is nonnegative; otherwise $0$).

**Answer: $q_1=4-\frac{q_2^*}{2}$**

smt-2023-power-3-09.title: Intersect best responses
smt-2023-power-3-09.body:
In equilibrium each quantity is a best response to the other: $q_1=4-\frac{q_2}2$ and $q_2=5-\frac{q_1}2$. Substituting: $q_1=4-\frac12\left(5-\frac{q_1}2\right)=\frac32+\frac{q_1}4$, so $q_1=2$ and $q_2=4$.

The price is $22-2\cdot6=10$. Firm one's profit is $10\cdot2-6\cdot2=8$; firm two's is $10\cdot4-2\cdot4=32$.

**Answer: $q_1=2$, $q_2=4$; profits $8$ and $32$**

smt-2023-power-3-10.title: Backward induction
smt-2023-power-3-10.body:
Firm two observes $q_1$ and best responds with $q_2(q_1)=5-\frac{q_1}2$ (Problem 3.8). Firm one anticipates this: its profit is $\left(22-2\left(q_1+5-\frac{q_1}2\right)\right)q_1-6q_1=(12-q_1)q_1-6q_1=-q_1(q_1-6)$, maximized at $q_1=3$.

The SPE is: firm one produces $q_1=3$, and firm two produces $q_2(q_1)=5-\frac{q_1}2$ after any $q_1$. On the equilibrium path $q_2=3.5$, the price is $22-2\cdot6.5=9$, and the profits are $9\cdot3-6\cdot3=9$ for firm one and $9\cdot3.5-2\cdot3.5=24.5$ for firm two.

**Answer: $q_1=3$ and $q_2(q_1)=5-q_1/2$ (outcome $(3,3.5)$)**

smt-2023-power-3-11.title: Backward induction
smt-2023-power-3-11.body:
Firm one observes $q_2$ and best responds with $q_1(q_2)=4-\frac{q_2}2$ (Problem 3.7). Firm two anticipates this: its profit is $\left(22-2\left(q_2+4-\frac{q_2}2\right)\right)q_2-2q_2=(14-q_2)q_2-2q_2=-q_2(q_2-12)$, maximized at $q_2=6$.

The SPE is: firm two produces $q_2=6$, and firm one produces $q_1(q_2)=4-\frac{q_2}2$ after any $q_2$. On the path $q_1=1$, the price is $22-2\cdot7=8$, and the profits are $8\cdot1-6\cdot1=2$ for firm one and $8\cdot6-2\cdot6=36$ for firm two.

**Answer: $q_2=6$ and $q_1(q_2)=4-q_2/2$ (outcome $(1,6)$)**

smt-2023-power-3-12.title: Set the costs equal
smt-2023-power-3-12.body:
For someone at meter $d$: $p_A+d=p_B+(500-d)$, so $2d=p_B-p_A+500$ and $d=\frac{p_B-p_A+500}{2}$.

**Answer: $d=\frac{p_B-p_A+500}2$**

smt-2023-power-3-13.title: Count customers
smt-2023-power-3-13.body:
Everyone at meters below $d=\frac{p_B-p_A+500}{2}$ buys from A, so A serves $d$ people and B serves $500-d=\frac{p_A-p_B+500}2$ people. Hence
$$u_A(p_A,p_B)=p_A\cdot\frac{p_B-p_A+500}{2},\qquad u_B(p_A,p_B)=p_B\cdot\frac{p_A-p_B+500}{2}.$$

smt-2023-power-3-14.title: Best responses
smt-2023-power-3-14.body:
$u_A=-\frac12p_A\left(p_A-(p_B+500)\right)$, a quadratic in $p_A$ maximized at $p_A=\frac{p_B+500}2=250+\frac{p_B}2$. Likewise stand B's best response is $p_B=250+\frac{p_A}{2}$.

In equilibrium both are best responses: $p_A=250+\frac12\left(250+\frac{p_A}2\right)=375+\frac{p_A}4$, so $p_A=500$ and $p_B=500$.

**Answer: both stands charge $500$**

smt-2023-power-3-15.title: Redo the best-response computation
smt-2023-power-3-15.body:
The indifferent meter $d'$ solves $p_A+\frac{d'}2=p_B+\frac{500-d'}2$, so $d'=p_B-p_A+250$. Profits: $u_A=p_A(p_B-p_A+250)=-p_A\left(p_A-(250+p_B)\right)$ and $u_B=p_B(p_A-p_B+250)$. Best responses: $p_A=125+\frac{p_B}2$ and $p_B=125+\frac{p_A}2$. Equilibrium: $p_A=p_B=250$.

At these prices $d'=250$, so each stand again serves $250$ people (as before, where $d=250$ too). In the old equilibrium each stand earned $500\cdot250=125{,}000$; now each earns $250\cdot250=62{,}500$. The prices are lower and the numbers served are unchanged, so the stands make less money.

**Answer: $p_A=p_B=250$; they make less money**
